newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada agrees to modify harmonized sales tax.
newsitem.headline: Canada agrees to modify harmonized sales tax.

text.p: The Canadian government said on Monday it would agree to modify its proposal to harmonize the sales tax in three Atlantic provinces so the law would not require tax-inclusive pricing.
Barry Campbell, the parliamentary secretary to the finance minister, told the House of Commons that the Liberal government would accept changes made to its bill by the unelected Senate.
Last week, Conservative senators stymied Finance Minister Paul Martin's plan to require tax-inclusive pricing in Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.

Martin had wanted to require companies to include the blended tax in their price tags rather than have cashiers add the tax at the cash register. But critics argued that national retailers would be forced to produce separate advertising and promotional material for the Atlantic region.
Conservative senators threatened to delay the bill indefinitely unless changes were made.

Once passed, the law would still bring the new 15 percent harmonized sales tax into force as scheduled on April 1. The law blends provincial retail taxes with the federal Goods and Services Tax as part of the government's attempt to keep its promise to replace the federal sales tax.
The tax allows overall tax rates to decline in the Atlantic provinces. The federal government has agreed to compensate the provincial governments for the lower tax level.
Tax-inclusive pricing will not start until more than half of Canada's population has joined the harmonized sales tax system.
